## On shaving the beard

**What is the ruling on shaving the beard, and may one trim it while it is short?**

Shaving the beard is among the things the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade, and he made known that trimming it with scissors and the like is not permitted, because it runs contrary to the letting-grow that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded. But if the beard grows very long and spreads out and becomes thick, then a person — if he is on hajj or on the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah) and has come out of the consecrated state of his hajj or his ʿumrah, whether by casting the pebbles at the Jamrat al-ʿAqabah on the day of Eid or by finishing the running (saʿy) of the ʿumrah — may take it in two handfuls and cut off what goes beyond them. Among the scholars are those who hold that if he takes one ample handful he has the right to cut off what goes beyond it; Ibn Umar and Abu Hurayrah used to do that.

## On the subject of visiting graves

**In the Prophet's words (peace and blessings be upon him) on this there is a way of reconciling the cursing of women who frequent the graves with his granting of permission. What are the particulars of that??**

The answer is that women's visiting of graves is a matter of disagreement among the people of knowledge. Some of the people of knowledge held it forbidden (ḥarām) without qualification, and adduced this report of the curse as their evidence. Others held that this is abrogated (mansūkh), because abrogation is established with regard to visiting graves.. For the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «I had forbidden you to visit the graves; now visit them, and do not utter anything unseemly.» And he said: «I had forbidden you to visit the graves; now indeed visit them, for they remind you of the hereafter.» This abrogation is, in principle, explicit in removing every prohibition that preceded it, whether the earlier prohibition was specific to women or not; because the permission here — rather, the command — is directed to men and women together, since he said: «visit them, for they remind you of the hereafter». "Visit them" is a command to all people, taking in men and women alike. This position — that of abrogation with respect to women — is the preponderant one, because the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) taught Aisha what to say when visiting graves; and had her visiting of graves been forbidden (ḥarām), he would not have taught her that.

## On what establishes the milk relationship

**A woman swore that she had breastfed me, and my parents denied it. What is the ruling on this?**

The people of knowledge have differed over what establishes the milk relationship (raḍāʿ), into four positions.

The Hanafis held that the threshold of testimony in the milk relationship is like the threshold of testimony generally, in all matters, so that the testimony of two upright men, or of one upright man and two women, is required. They explained that God — glorified and exalted is He — set the threshold of testimony in the Qur'an in that way, for He said: {And call two witnesses to witness from among your men; and if there are not two men, then one man and two women} (Sūrat al-Baqarah 2:282), and He said concerning divorce: {And call to witness two men of probity from among you, and establish the testimony for God} (Sūrat al-Ṭalāq 65:2). On this basis the threshold of testimony is always two upright men, or one man and two women.

The Shafi'is held that the milk relationship is established by the testimony of four women who are qualified to testify, because it is a matter belonging to women and not to men, and in testimony two women stand in the place of each man.

The Malikis held that the milk relationship is established by the testimony of two women of probity, because plurality is a condition in testimony but not in the transmission of reports; and this class of matter is proper to women, so that once plurality is achieved, enough has been achieved by it for the substance of the question to be established, this being among the matters that rest on probable evidence.

The Hanbalis held that the milk relationship is established by the testimony of a single woman. The Hanbalis adduced as evidence what al-Bukhari brought out in the Ṣaḥīḥ, and others besides him, from the report of Uqbah ibn al-Harith — may God be pleased with him — who said: I married Umm Yahya bint Abi Ihab ibn Aziz, and a black woman came and said, "I breastfed Uqbah and the woman he has married." I said: I did not know that, and you did not tell me. So I sent to the family of Abu Ihab to ask them, and they said: we did not know that. So I mounted my riding camel and came to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) in Medina and asked him, and he said: «How can that be, when it has already been said?» And in one transmission: «Part from her, for there is no good for you in her.» So I parted from her, and she married a man other than me.

The Hanbalis adduce this report as evidence that the milk relationship is established by the testimony of a single woman, even if she is the nursing woman herself, and even if the infant's parents call her a liar; for the parents of Abu Ihab's daughter denied that that woman had breastfed her, and said: we did not know that. Yet despite that, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade him to continue in that marriage and said: part from her, for there is no good for you in her, and said: how can that be, when it has already been said?

The Malikis, for their part, saw this report as evidence that the milk relationship is not established by the testimony of a single woman, because he said: part from her; and you know that parting is divorce, and divorce comes about only after a valid marriage contract, by the words of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): «A person has no divorce and no manumission in what he does not own.» This entails that the marriage was valid, because he said "part from her", the meaning of which is that the marriage that took place is recognised in law, so that a separation within it is needed, and that separation is divorce — which amounts to holding the contract valid. And it is well known that a woman who is forbidden in marriage cannot lawfully be contracted, and the contract is not valid in any respect whatever; so had the milk relationship been established, the marriage would not have been conceivable in the first place.

Even so, the Malikis took account of the disagreement and held it recommended (mandūb) to keep clear on the testimony of a single woman. This is with respect to marriage, that is, on the side of prohibition. As for the side of declaring lawful — that is, the spread of the marriage impediment, as when he shakes hands with this woman who has claimed that she breastfed him — then if his parents deny it, the prudent course is that he not shake hands with her, and that he not act upon this milk relationship in what concerns the affirmative side. As for the prohibitive side, which is the negative side, we have already mentioned the disagreement within it; as for the affirmative side, he is not to act upon this milk relationship.

A single person may have two aspects to him. For when Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abd ibn Zam'ah brought a dispute before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) over a boy — Abd saying that he was a son to his father, born upon his bed from his slave woman, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas saying that his brother Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas had charged him that the boy was his son — the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) adjudged him to Abd ibn Zam'ah and said: «The child belongs to the bed, and for the fornicator is the stone.» Yet despite that he commanded Sawdah bint Zam'ah — and she is a Mother of the Believers — to veil herself from him. The meaning of this is that he took account of both aspects: in view of his resemblance to Utbah ibn Abi Waqqas, he having been Utbah's son through fornication, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded Sawdah to veil herself from him; and in view of his having been born upon the other man's bed, the other man not having disowned him, he being the son of his slave woman upon his bed, lineage follows that — and for that reason he adjudged him to Abd ibn Zam'ah, and commanded Sawdah to veil herself from him.

## The ruling on shaving customers' beards

**Is it permissible to shave customers' beards? Many customers shave their beard along with their head, and if I refuse to do it for him I lose the trade.**

It appears that the questioner is one of those who practise the barber's trade, so he is not asking about shaving his own beard but about occupying himself with shaving the beards of others. The answer is that occupying oneself with that is part of cooperating in sin and transgression, so it is not lawful to occupy oneself with it. God Most High has said: {And cooperate in righteousness and God-consciousness (taqwā), and do not cooperate in sin and transgression} (Sūrat al-Māʾidah 5:2).

A person must know that God is the Provider, the Possessor of Strength, the Firm; that provision is in God's hand and has already been written; that the pens have been lifted and the pages have dried upon what is to be. God — glorified and exalted is He — sends an angel to the foetus while it is in its mother's womb, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) explained, and he is commanded with four words: to write its provision, its appointed term, its deeds, and whether it is wretched or happy. For that reason a person ought to know that provision has been written and neither increases nor decreases, and that he must be moderate in the seeking of it, as the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «God has written for every soul its provision, so be mindful of God and be moderate in seeking.» And in the other report: «The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart that no soul will die until it has completed its provision, so be mindful of God and be moderate in seeking.» Part of moderation in seeking is that it be from what is lawful; seeking provision from what is forbidden (ḥarām) is no part of moderation in seeking. For what is with God is not to be sought by means of the forbidden — what is with God is not sought by disobeying Him.

## The ruling on being alone together in a car

**Is it permissible for a woman to ride alone with the owner of the car, in the middle of the city for instance?**

If she rides in the back and is not immediately beside the owner of the car, and this is at a time when the streets are crowded — that is, there are people in them — then this is not a case of seclusion (khalwah), so long as no ground for suspicion arises. But if this is at suspect times, such as in the dark, or when the streets are empty of people, or she is in the seat next to him such that their limbs may easily touch, then this is forbidden (ḥarām), because the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) warned against the breaths of men coming close to the breaths of women.

## The ruling on a woman who acknowledged having breastfed a little girl and then denied it

**A woman had a small daughter; she went out and left her with another woman, and when she came back the woman told her that she had breastfed the girl. She became angry with her, so she then denied that she had breastfed her. Is her first statement to be relied upon, or her second, given that there is no witness?**

When a witness retracts his testimony, it becomes void (bāṭil). So if the woman has retracted her statement and there is no witness besides her, then no weight attaches to it, and her first statement alone, which she has retracted, does not establish it.

## Some rulings on offering condolences

**Does the presence of the deceased's family in their house count as sitting to receive condolences, or not? And is that for three days, or not?**

Gathering at the house of the deceased's family was counted as ritual wailing in the time of the Companions, may God be pleased with them. What is meant by that is gathering in assemblies where people come together for food and for talk, so that the clamour in them grows great and the deceased's family are put to heavy expense. This sort is part of the wailing that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade, and from whose practitioners he declared himself free.

As for gathering at their house to offer condolences — as when a delegation of people comes to them to offer condolences, or a person comes to them to offer condolences and a number of people gather at their house — this is not among what the law forbids; but they are not to eat, nor to drink, nor to gather for the repetition of much talk, for that is what is counted as wailing. Their sitting in order to offer condolences is part of cooperating in righteousness and God-consciousness, for God — glorified and exalted is He — has prescribed for us that we cooperate in righteousness and God-consciousness. Offering condolences is among the things that bind the ties of kinship and increase love, and it means urging the bereaved to patient endurance.

So if it is done in the manner the law prescribes — that is, mentioning the merit and the reward God has attached to patience, mentioning the good that one knows of the deceased, and supplicating for him and for his family after his death — then this is the permissible (jāʾiz) form of condolence, and it is recommended (mandūb). The deceased's family accepting it is a case of accepting kindness and accepting a good turn, and accepting a good turn is among the noble traits of character. Refusing a gift is not among the noble traits of character; refusing condolence is not among the noble traits of character; refusing a sick-visit is not among the noble traits of character. For that reason, accepting it is part of cooperating in righteousness and God-consciousness — but on condition that it is held within these limits the law sets; for if it goes beyond the bound the law permits, it becomes a breach of the law, and cooperating in it becomes part of cooperating in sin and transgression.

## The ruling on giving the feeding of sixty poor people to a single poor person

**Can the feeding of sixty poor people be given to a single poor person?**

The position of the majority of the people of knowledge is to give weight to the number and to its specifier both, for God mentioned a number with a specifier, saying: {then the feeding of sixty poor people} (Sūrat al-Mujādilah 58:4). The number is His word "sixty" and the specifier is His word "poor person". Giving weight to the two together is the position of the majority of the people of knowledge, so that feeding this number is required, each poor person receiving a mudd.

Abu Hanifah held that weight is given to the number without giving weight to the specifier; he said that the specifier follows the number, and that therefore it is lawful for a single poor person to be given sixty mudds. Abu Hanifah alone is the one who permitted giving a single poor person sixty mudds and held that this discharges the obligation. The majority of the people of knowledge gave weight to the two words together and held that sixty poor people must be given, each poor person being given a mudd. The position of the majority is the one that accords with the plain sense of the verse, so it is more preponderant and more fitting.

## The ruling on reducing the value of the blood money

**Is it permissible to reduce the value of the blood money (diyah) that the Lawgiver has fixed, on the basis that this is in the interest of the tribe, as some people hold?**

No. For God — glorified and exalted is He — has set limits which it is not lawful to overstep, nor to fall short of; and what the Lawgiver has fixed of the determined quantities (al-muqaddarāt) may not lawfully be reduced under any circumstance whatever. The blood money — the blood money for a man — is one thousand gold dinars, or ten thousand silver dirhams, or one hundred she-camels. This is the Messenger of God's (peace and blessings be upon him) fixing of the blood monies in the letter of Amr ibn Hazm, and it is a matter of agreement among the Muslims.

## Valuing the blood money in currency

**What is the amount of the blood money today in ouguiya?**

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) imposed the blood money upon the people of gold as one thousand dinars, upon the people of silver as ten thousand dirhams, and upon the people of camels as one hundred camels; he made it fall into five age-classes, and did not include males in it. As for the blood money for quasi-deliberate error, he made it heavier by setting it in three classes, as comes in the report of al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah, from Uqbah ibn Aws, from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-'As, that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The one slain by quasi-deliberate error — by the whip, the staff or the stone — for him there are one hundred camels, forty of them pregnant with their young in their bellies. That is because Satan leaps among people, so that blood is shed where there is no rancour and no bearing of arms."

On this basis the scholars differed as to whether the blood money goes back to one base or to three bases. If we say it is one base, is its base the camels, as a number of the imams held, or is its base the gold, as some of the Zahiris held? And if we say it goes back to three bases, then gold is a base, silver is a base and camels are a base, and everything else is assessed by analogy (qiyās) upon them: other animals are assessed by analogy upon the camels by price, as with cattle and sheep, and all other currencies are assessed by analogy upon the gold. So the value of one thousand gold dinars in ouguiya, for example, is what is taken into account in that way: one looks to the thousand dinars and does not look to the value of the camels, because the ouguiya is closer to gold than it is to camels.

There is disagreement on this question between the Maliki jurists and others: the Malikis differed as to whether the blood money has one base or three. Some of the Shafi'is held that the blood money has five bases, having regard to the practice of Umar ibn al-Khattab, for he imposed it upon the people of trade in garments, and imposed it upon the people of cattle in cattle likewise. So this is a matter of disagreement. In general, if we wish to value it, the most preponderant course in it and the closest is that the dinars be valued: one thousand dinars are valued in the money of the currency, and whatever that comes to is the blood money of a Muslim.

## The ruling on prompting the deceased after death

**Does prompting the deceased after his death have a basis in the Sunnah, and if the answer is yes, what part of it is established?**

Prompting is of two kinds: prompting during life and prompting after death.

As for prompting during life, it is established from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) that he commanded that the dying person be prompted with the testimony that there is no god but God — that is, that it be said in his presence while he can hear: "There is no god but God", so that perhaps his last words will be "there is no god but God". It is said before him, and he is not told "say it", lest he refuse; rather "there is no god but God" is said in his presence. If he says it once, one falls silent and does not repeat it to him, unless he afterwards speaks some word about worldly matters, in which case it is said to him once more so that he may say it.

As for prompting after death, a weak (ḍaʿīf) report has come concerning it, which Ibn Majah brought out in the Sunan and others besides him, from the report of Abu Umamah Sudayy ibn Ajlan al-Bahili, may God be pleased with him. In it is the command to prompt the dead after death: that a person stand at the head of one of them and say, "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so, when the two angels come to you, say to them what you left the world upon — namely that you bear witness that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and that you are content with God as Lord, with Islam as religion, and with Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) as Messenger."

This report is weak. The dead do not hear the speech of the living, because a barrier has been placed between them, as He said, exalted is He: {And behind them is a barrier (barzakh) until the day they are raised up} (Sūrat al-Muʾminūn 23:100). They hear only what God causes them to hear of it. That is why God Most High said to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): {Truly you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away in flight} (Sūrat al-Naml 27:80); and He said, exalted is He: {Truly you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they are warned}; and He said, exalted is He: {And you are not one who can make those in the graves hear; you are only a warner} (Sūrat Fāṭir 35:22–23).

As for God's causing them to hear, He causes them to hear the questioning of the two angels and returns their spirits to them for the answer. Likewise He returned their spirits to the people of the well on the day of Badr, until they heard the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) words to them, and his rebuking of them was a species of the punishment of the grave. That is why the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: you are not better able to hear what I say than they are. He addressed them with what would abase them, saying: have you found what your Lord promised to be true? For we have found what our Lord promised us to be true. That was an abasement of them, just as the questioning of the two angels is in the first place. This comes from God, and none but God Most High brings it about that it is heard.

As for his words (peace and blessings be upon him) in the report on the questioning — "and indeed he hears the sound of their sandals" — many of the people of knowledge have explained it to mean that they are still so near to him that anyone with him would hear the sound of their sandals, if anyone had remained with him.

Even so, despite the weakness of the report on prompting after death, a number of scholars have acted upon it, and acting upon a weak report in a case of this sort is itself a matter of disagreement. Therefore, if a person does it, the principle is that he should supplicate much for the deceased. It has come from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) that one supplicates at the grave for steadfastness once the deceased has been laid in it, and that he commanded this; for he used to say: (Ask for him steadfastness, for he is being questioned now), and in some reports: (Ask for your companion steadfastness, for he is being questioned now). A number of the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) Companions would form a ring around the grave and supplicate for its occupant. Muslim brought out in the Ṣaḥīḥ that Amr ibn al-'As — may God be pleased with him — charged his son that when he died they should stand by his grave for as long as it takes a camel to be slaughtered and its meat distributed; and perhaps by that he meant their supplicating for him in those moments, to an extent that would not burden them.

## The ruling on reciting the Qur'an for the dead

**Is it permissible to recite the Qur'an over the deceased — that is, what people call the salkah?**

Reciting the Qur'an and making a gift of its reward to the deceased is called talḥīq, which is the attaching of the reward of what a person recites to someone who has died. The people of knowledge have differed over it. Malik and Abu Hanifah held that it does not reach him, because it is an act of the body, and so is not like voluntary charity (ṣadaqah) and the like among things that are separable from the person. Malik's position, then, is that it does not reach him. Therefore a person should do what does reach him, namely voluntary charity or supplication. The erudite Muhammad Mawlud — the mercy of God be upon him — said:

*The reward of food and of supplication, if they are given for the deceased — there is no disagreement that they reach him.*

As for matters other than that, there is disagreement over whether they reach him or not. People's gathering at the house of the deceased's family is a form of wailing, and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade wailing and declared himself free of whoever does it; and some of his Companions made clear that they used to count gathering at the house of the deceased's family as wailing. Gathering at the house of the deceased's family includes gathering to recite the Qur'an, so that ought not to take place, and people ought not to do it nor to make a display of it, for it is among the newly invented innovations in religion (bidʿah).

## Does the suckling of a woman who bore a child out of fornication create the marriage impediment

**Is the milk relationship valid with the milk of a child who has no father?**

Yes, the marriage impediment spreads through that suckling on the side of that child's mother; and he has no father, so that the impediment might spread on his father's side. For the milk relationship is an act, and it arises from milk; so if milk is produced, even with no marriage at all — as when milk appears in a woman's breast without any marriage — that milk spreads the marriage impediment, on the preponderant view, provided the child derives nourishment from it. For the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) laid down as a condition in suckling only that nourishment be derived, for he said: «Suckling is only that which is from hunger.» And he said: «What builds up the bone and causes the flesh to grow creates the impediment.» And he said: «One suck does not create the impediment, nor two sucks, nor one draught, nor two draughts; but rather what opens up the bowels.» So the thing that opens up the bowels and benefits the child in its nourishment is what the marriage impediment spreads through.

## What establishes the milk relationship

**A person of whom it was said that a woman had breastfed him, though he never knew her alive; his mother, his grandmother and his maternal aunts denied it, but his father thinks that the woman did breastfeed him. What is the ruling?**

If no one whose testimony would establish it testifies to it, then the presumption is non-existence: the default position regarding this milk relationship is that it does not exist, until a sufficient number of witnesses to establish it testify to it. We have already mentioned that the threshold of proof in suckling is disputed between the schools. With the Malikis, the milk relationship is established only by the testimony of two women, even if one of the two is the nursing woman; with the Hanbalis it is established by the testimony of a single woman; with the Shafi'is it is not established except by the testimony of four women; and with the Hanafis it is not established except by the testimony of one upright man and two women. On this basis, if this milk relationship is not established and no one has testified to it, no weight attaches to it.

## Some scholars shave their beards — what is their evidence for that?

**Today we find many scholars shaving their beards, especially in the east. What is the evidence they rely upon in this question? And is there disagreement over the amount that may be taken from the beard's length and its breadth?**

As regards everyone below the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), his action is no proof. Only the action of the one preserved from error is a proof; as for one who is not preserved from error, his action is no proof, even were he Abu Bakr or Umar, because a contravention can occur from him. God Most High said concerning the people of Uhud: {Truly those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met — Satan only made them slip, because of some of what they had earned; and God has certainly pardoned them} [Āl ʿImrān 155]. If the Companions of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) stand in this position, what then of those below them?

For that reason a person ought not to be taken in by people's actions, for people have excuses in their actions, and those actions may be expiated by some of their other good deeds. Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah — may God have mercy on him — said that many of the Companions of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) from whom some contraventions occurred are the people most deserving of forgiveness, because of their closeness to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), their struggle alongside him, their pledge to him, their support of him, and their precedence in Islam; so they were more deserving of forgiveness than anyone else. Therefore the best construction is to be sought for all of them.

The same applies to anyone known for knowledge, uprightness, rectitude and goodness, in any age whatever: he is to be construed in that way. So if we see from him a contravention of the Sunnah, or an outward act contrary to the law, we count it among the sins that are fit to be expiated — God willing, his other good deeds will expiate them. Ibn al-Qayyim — may God have mercy on him — said: the slips of the scholars are filth, and they themselves are seas; and when water reaches two qullahs it does not carry impurity. So their slips are as filth cast upon the shores of the seas, and it does them no harm:

*What harm did it do to Taghlib of Wa'il, whether you lampooned them, or made water where the two seas clash together?*

So this is something that has no effect.

## The ruling on shaving the tuft below the lip

**What is the ruling on shaving the tuft below the lower lip (ʿanfaqah)?**

Its ruling is the ruling of the beard; and a group said its ruling is the ruling of the moustache. Al-Bukhari brought out in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in the report of Ibn Umar, that he used to trim closely and to take from these two. "He used to trim closely" — that is, he trimmed his moustache closely — "and to take from these two". There is disagreement here over the demonstrative, over the demonstrative pronoun, because he did not specify anything. It was said: what is meant by "these two" is the upper and the lower edge of the mouth, that is, the moustache and the tuft below the lip — and this makes it permissible to take from it. And it was said: "he takes from these two" means the two corners of the mouth, which are where the lips meet. Shaykh Muhammad Ali — may God have mercy on him — said on this question:

*al-Bukhari's words, "and he used to trim closely" — "he takes these two", with the wāw of conjunction* — until he says — *and that is where the lips meet, where one who is clean cleans his mouth; that is the most fitting sense in which to construe it* ................................... — until he says — *so begin with it first of all.*

That is, it is the position most fit to be begun with. So the most fitting of the positions, in the Shaykh's view, is that it means where the lips meet, where one who is clean cleans his mouth. Yet despite that, it has also been explained as the tuft below the lip and the moustache. On this basis the matter concerning it is not strict — the matter concerning the tuft below the lip is not strict.

## Some rulings on hire and leasing

**A worker who works in the house and whose wage runs by the month — if he leaves, does he have a right to it or not?**

When a person hires a worker for a defined period of time — whether defined by express stipulation or defined by custom (ʿurf), it being well known that the custom of the people of our country is that a worker is hired for a month — then if he has begun work with you and has spoiled nothing in it, and his work was to the specification required, he has become entitled to his wage for that whole month. If he stops part-way through, and it is he who is held up — because of illness, or the illness of one of his family, or a need of his own that required him to ask leave — then he is entitled only to the wage for what he worked of that month. But if it is you who has no further need of his service, and you have moved away from this place and no longer need this worker, then you must pay him a full month's wage. That is why Khalil — may God have mercy on him — said: "And the hire becomes binding upon enablement."

Whoever rents one of the houses — and it is well known that houses are rented by the month — so you rented a flat for a fixed sum of 35,000 ouguiya and stayed in it only a week, and then it seemed good to you to move away from this place: the rent is owed in full to its owner, and you for your part may lodge in it whomever you wish for the remainder of the month, because you took ownership of the yield of this flat for a month, and the owner of the flat took ownership of its rent. So this maxim must be observed, namely "the hire becomes binding upon enablement" — that when this contract has been concluded, the rent falls due by the mere fact of enablement, even if you have not taken all of what you rented it for.

Here attention must also be drawn to a matter that is needed, namely that the thing hired may permissibly be let on, in what the law calls sub-letting. Sub-letting, which is familiar to lawyers, is this: if you rented a house at a specified price, you may let it to another, even at a price higher than the price at which you rented it. This type is sub-letting, and it is permissible (jāʾiz) in the Sharia — but on one condition, namely that the one to whom it is let, the second party, put it to no use other than the like of what you rented it for. If you rented the flat in order to live in it, then it is not permissible for you to let it to someone who will make it a car garage, nor to someone who will make it a milling premises, because the owner does not wish to let it for that, and he is its owner. So you may let it to someone who will use it for the same purpose for which you rented it. If it was a commercial premises for a particular kind of trade, you must let it to someone who will exploit it in that same kind, and you may not let it for those trades for which letting is not wanted, such as a car garage, clothes-washing and the like; for people do not usually wish to let their houses for these, because they lead to their being dirtied and damaged.

## The ruling on maintenance contracts

**A group of owners of large haulage vehicles agree with an expert in vehicle repair, paying him a monthly sum for each vehicle. If the vehicle does not break down they do not reduce his payment; and if the vehicle breaks down badly and the expert spends a great deal of time and effort repairing it, they do not increase it beyond that sum. What is the ruling on this contract?**

This contract is what is called, in the usage of today's lawyers, a maintenance contract. Maintenance contracts include those relating to buildings; those relating to appliances, vehicles, aircraft and ships; and those relating to streets, roads and the like. It has become settled in the usage of people today that maintenance contracts must contain a delimitation — that is, that the extent of the maintainer's liability (ḍamān) be delimited. For example, if the maintenance contract is on a vehicle and its engine fails altogether — the engine block has broken, the engine has broken — then this does not fall within the maintainer's liability, by custom, in people's usual practice. Likewise if the maintenance contract relates to a computer and the RAM burns out, for instance, or the hard disk fails such that he cannot restore it: this device is no longer fit for maintenance, so this does not fall within the maintainer's liability. That applies rather to the ordinary parts, whose failure and replacement are frequent.

This contract doubtless contains a very clear unacceptable uncertainty (gharar), namely that the thing covered may break down and may not, as was mentioned in the question about the vehicle. But if this uncertainty is slight — in that breakdowns in the matter are frequent — then it is overlooked. From this it follows that, of the maintenance contracts concluded today, some are permissible (mubāḥ) and some are forbidden (muḥarram).

The permissible among them is the case where a person has real property, for example, and knows that at every interval the paintwork needs renewing — because this paint has a certain life under humidity and the alternation of heat and cold, and must inevitably come away, so that the building needs maintenance by removing the existing paint and applying it afresh — and likewise the doors and the windows, and similarly the air conditioners and the like, among the things that require periodic maintenance. What is spent on maintenance in matters such as these is customarily known, and the period they last is known: in many countries it is known that the maintenance of large buildings falls every six months, for example. So this type, where it is known, is among the permissible matters (jāʾiz), and the uncertainty in it is overlooked, like the uncertainty in a building contract in the first place. For as to a building contract: is it not the case that in the blocks with which one builds, the quantity of shell aggregate put into them and the quantity of cement put into them vary, and a person cannot regulate that precisely? So this kind of slight uncertainty is excused.

The same applies to the breaking down of vehicles. If the vehicles belong to government departments and the like, and their breaking down follows from the work they do, then it is known that this vehicle performs such-and-such a service and covers so many miles each month; and it is known that these miles and this particular service require a determinate maintenance, namely changing the oils every 3,000 or 4,000 kilometres, which is determinate; and it is known when it will cover this number of miles, so that when it has covered these miles the oils are changed for it. And at the second change the filters are also changed — the small filters, the oil filter and the petrol filter; if, for instance, it runs on diesel, all the filters must be changed at the second oil change. This type is known by custom, and a maintenance contract upon it is permissible.

But what relates to repairing the engines, and repairing the gearing — what is called, for example, the boîte de vitesses or the boîte de transfert, or the like — this kind does not fall within a maintenance contract, because it is a case of uncertainty: the vehicle may last long and not need it, and it may need it because of some fault on the driver's part. Therefore the maintenance contract must be bounded by limits that prevent gross uncertainty; slight uncertainty is excused in a case of this sort.

Several controlling criteria have been laid down for the maintenance contract, which can be referred to. Among these criteria are, first, avoiding gross uncertainty; and among them delimitation in time; and among them delimitation in place, by defining it. These criteria must be gone over, so that the contract may be properly regulated. People today enter into very strange contracts, containing a very great deal of uncertainty, so that the maintenance contract is nothing but the consuming of people's property wrongfully: you pay out money for repairing your car when you had no need of repair at all. This kind of contract, which exposes one to such a degree of uncertainty, is forbidden (ḥarām); for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade the sale involving uncertainty, and consuming people's property wrongfully is forbidden. Therefore the contract must be regulated by clear criteria that reduce the proportion of uncertainty in it.

Here attention must be drawn to a matter, namely that factories and vehicle owners — and likewise the government departments that repair roads or buildings — customarily know what is needed for maintenance. The evidence for that is that they put an item in the budget specifically for maintenance. Every government department, and every company, knows what is needed for maintenance and so allocates it a budget item according to the expectation of those with expertise. We know that the spending may not be kept strictly within the items, and that funds may be taken from one item to another; but it is known that the estimate was in the first place made on the basis of expertise. And if it was on the basis of expertise, that entails the removal of the ignorance the law guards against; for what the law guards against is the uncertainty whose cause is ignorance. So if there is a scientific estimate founded upon custom and experience, this suffices to remove the uncertainty and to make this contract permissible (mubāḥ).

## The ruling on shaving the sides of the beard

**Does the prohibition that has come regarding shaving the beard take in the sides of the face or not?**

The beard is what grows upon the lower bone, which is the lower jaw — that is the laḥy. The laḥy is the lower bone, that is, the lower jaw; so whatever grows upon it is beard. The place where the two jawbones meet is called the chin and is not called beard. The beard is all of this; as for the place where the two jawbones meet, that is called the chin only. That is why Ibn al-Murahhal — may God have mercy on him — said in his versification of the Faṣīḥ of Tha'lab:

*And the laḥy is the bone of the jaw, and it is the lower one; and form its plural as alḥin when they are few. And liḥyah, with an i-vowel; and the plural is al-liḥā with an i-vowel if you wish, or al-luḥā if you wish.*

So what has come from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) of the command to let the beards grow full takes in what grows upon this bone, from opposite one ear to opposite the other. Whatever grows upon this bone is beard.

## The ruling on slaughtering after the slaughter of the imam of a mosque where the Friday prayer is not held

**What is the ruling on a group of people who slaughtered their sacrifices before the slaughter of the Friday preacher, because they had prayed the Eid prayer behind another imam, and when he slaughtered they slaughtered with his slaughter — given that this latter is the imam of a mosque where the Friday prayer is not held at all, and the preacher is not a mile distant from them?**

What counts is the imam of the Eid prayer. So if the imam has prayed the Eid prayer and slaughtered his sacrifice (uḍḥiyah), then it has become lawful for whoever prayed behind him to slaughter his own sacrifice; and the same applies to one who did not pray the Eid prayer, where that imam was the nearest to him. Some of the people of knowledge held that, where the mosques are several and the Eid prayers are several in a single town, what counts is the first of them: so if the first has prayed and slaughtered, slaughter becomes permissible for all the inhabitants of that town. This is because the operative cause (ʿillah) upon which the law has hung the ruling must be an apparent, well-defined attribute — that is the definition of the operative cause among the legal theorists: it is the apparent, well-defined attribute to which the Lawgiver has attached the ruling. Rulings cannot be attached to something unknown or wavering. Therefore we cannot attach it to one imam out of all the imams, nor to one mosque among the mosques. Since the Eid prayer may permissibly be repeated — a number of congregations may pray it in a single town and a single village — then when any imam among them has slaughtered, the earlier imam makes the slaughter of the sacrifice lawful for those behind him.

There remains what relates to trading on Friday, for trading becomes lawful at the end of the Friday prayer. So if it is like a town in which the Friday prayers are several, it has been said that the first of the imams to give the closing salutation is the one who makes it lawful — because the operative cause, as we said, is an apparent, well-defined attribute, so it must be determinate; and we cannot fix upon the last imam, because that is among the unknowns, whereas the first imam is among the knowns. Therefore they said: the prohibition attaches to the first imam who gives the salutation; so once the first imam in the town you are in has given the salutation, trading has been made lawful.

## The ruling on shaving the beard

**What is the ruling on shaving the beard?**

The answer to it has already been given in the previous episode, and we mentioned that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded that the beard be left to grow full.

## The ruling on eating from the property of one who earns his living by al-raqīq

**If you would go into detail on the matter of eating from the property of one who earns his living by al-raqīq: some of the sisters have husbands who earn by this, so how are they to stop eating from his property?**

We have already mentioned that one who has several sources of earning may be dealt with without qualification, and that his gifts may be accepted; for one the greater part of whose property is lawful — where lawful and forbidden are mixed together in his property — his property may be used. But as for one whose property is entirely from what is forbidden, it is not permissible to accept his gifts except in exchange for a consideration. And if the woman is his wife and finds what makes her independent of his maintenance, then let her make do with that; and if she does not find what makes her independent, then let her take it, and let that be on the ground of necessity (ḍarūrah) only.

## The ruling on covering the feet for women

**If you would speak about socks: one of the sisters, after the instruction to cover the feet, argued against me that you had not declared uncovering the feet forbidden.**

The two feet are a matter of disagreement — whether they are part of what must be covered (ʿawrah) or not — with many positions among the people of knowledge.

The first position: that the feet are part of the ʿawrah, because they are like the rest of the body. Some of the Malikis and some of the Shafi'is held this.

The second position: that the feet are not part of the ʿawrah at all, neither their upper nor their lower surface. This is the position of al-Muzani, of the companions of al-Shafi'i.

The third position: that their lower surface is not part of the ʿawrah and their upper surface is. This is the school of Abu Hanifah.

The fourth position: that if they bear a dye they are part of the ʿawrah, and if they bear no dye they are not.

But the report of Umm Salamah — may God be pleased with her — with which she disputed with the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) when he commanded the men not to go beyond the ankles and said, "what is below the ankles is in the Fire"; she said: "O Messenger of God, what are the women to do with their heels?" He said: "Let them let it down a span." She said: "Then they will be uncovered." He said: "Let them let it down a cubit" — in this there is an absence of strictness on the part of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) in the covering of the feet.

But there is no doubt that covering the feet is a meritorious act (faḍīlah) in any case: whether we say that they are part of the ʿawrah, in which case it is obligatory (wājib); or that they fall below that, in which case it is a matter of prudence and of the noble traits of character. So it is among the meritorious traits of character and deeds, and it ought not to be neglected.

## The legally prescribed covering

**Debate often goes round among women on the question of the legally prescribed covering (ḥijāb): some say the woman is entirely ʿawrah, some make an exception for the face and the hands, some say the garment must be black. What is the preponderant position, and is the more scrupulous course to cover the face and the hands and to adopt a black garment?**

The ruling of the law requires of women that they submit to the command of God and His Messenger, and that their worship not be a following of caprice and of the inclinations of the self. That is why God Most High said: {It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair} (Sūrat al-Aḥzāb 33:36). Therefore, when the command of God and His Messenger has come, it is for everyone to say: we hear and we obey.

God — mighty and majestic — commanded women to cover themselves, and did not specify by an explicit text (naṣṣ) what they are obliged to cover; and the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) likewise commanded them. But it is established from him (peace and blessings be upon him), in eight sound (ṣaḥīḥ) reports, that women in his presence would uncover their faces and likewise their hands. This indicates that the face and the hands are not part of the ʿawrah — and by "the hands" what is meant is the palms only. It is likewise established from him (peace and blessings be upon him) that he would speak with them and converse with them with their faces showing; this indicates that faces are not part of the ʿawrah. Likewise, by scholarly consensus (ijmāʿ) they are not obliged to cover their faces and their palms in the prayer; this indicates that the face and the palms in the prayer are not part of the ʿawrah.

As for the colour of the garment, no explicit text and no command has come concerning it, so any colour she wishes is lawful for the woman. But she is barred from going out in whatever draws attention, whether black or other than black; for whatever draws attention by its beauty or by its scent is prohibited...

If she fears temptation (fitnah), or temptation is feared on her account, it becomes obligatory (wājib) for her to cover her face. And if temptation is feared even with the face covered, it becomes obligatory for her not to go out of the house. And if temptation is feared on account of the clothing even though she is completely covered, it becomes obligatory for her not to go out of the house at all. For once temptation has arisen, cutting it off becomes obligatory without qualification.

## The evidence for the prohibition of musical instruments

**I know that stringed instruments are forbidden; I would like a basis for that from the hadiths and the Qur'an.**

As regards stringed instruments, which are instruments of diversion: musical instruments are forbidden. The evidence for that from the Qur'an is the words of God Most High: {And among people is he who buys diverting talk, so as to lead astray from the path of God without knowledge} (Sūrat Luqmān 31:6); and it is established from Ibn Mas'ud that he swore that this verse was revealed concerning singing. The evidence for it from the Sunnah is what is established in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "There will be a people at the end of time, of this community, who will be transformed into apes and swine; they will hold lawful wine, silk and musical instruments." 

## The ruling on women visiting graves

**What is the ruling on women visiting graves, given that she visits her parents and travels from a distant place?**

The Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade visiting graves in the earliest period of Islam, when people vied with one another by their dead and used to count them up and boast of them. Then afterwards, once the sura had been revealed — {Vying for more has diverted you, until you visited the graves} (Sūrat al-Takāthur 102:1–2) — the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «I had forbidden you to visit the graves; now visit them, for they remind you of the hereafter.» And in one transmission: now visit them, and do not utter hujr — and hujr is foul speech.

This report is general as regards men and women. The evidence for that is what is established from the report of Aisha, that she asked the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) what she should say when she visited the dead, and he taught her to say: «Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people; and we, God willing, are joining you. May God set your fear at rest and calm your loneliness, and make Paradise the meeting-place between us and you. May God have mercy on those of us who have gone before and those who remain.» Likewise Aisha — may God be pleased with her — missed the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) one night while he was with her, and went out looking for him, and found him standing facing the heads of the graveyard, supplicating for them. She stood behind him and supplicated with what he supplicated, then went back and arrived before him; and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) knew that she had gone out looking for him, and asked her, and she told him what had happened.

On this basis, if a woman has her dead near her, there is no objection to her visiting them — but she should not stand at every grave; rather she should stand before the graveyard, call the hereafter to mind, and supplicate for them with what the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) taught Aisha to supplicate with. At that point the woman gains three things, or gains from three aspects, which should be taken in order.

The first aspect: that she call to mind that the grave is a pit among the pits of the Fire, or a garden among the gardens of Paradise; that news of its occupant has been cut off from the people of this world; that the people of the graves are imprisoned in their graves — near neighbours who do not visit one another, and in a loneliness from which they are never released; captives of sins, never released; near neighbours who do not visit one another; and that they, here in this state, are either in a garden among the gardens of Paradise or in a pit among the pits of the Fire. The grave is the first of the stations of the hereafter, and it is greater than everything before it, and everything after it is greater than it. This is the first admonition.

The second admonition: that she call to mind the condition of those who have been buried in these graves, so that news of them has been cut off from people. They used to be thought of as among the influential, among those who are trusted and to whom works and affairs are committed; and yet for all that, their families came to dispose of their belongings after them. The person who was grasping and miserly — his money came to be shared out among people. The person who guarded his secrets and his own private affairs — his chests came to be divided among people and his keys into their hands; and so too his own clothes are worn by someone other than him. He has departed from this world, and having been one who feared everything, he has come to be in the most desolate of dwellings and the most fearful of them, as the poet said, lamenting his wife:

*How is it that you have come to dwell — you who were so very timid — in a land where the brave man dwells and is seized with fear? You have left behind a little girl, pitied, who does not know what grieving for you is, that she might grieve; and when I hear her whimpering in the night, the channels of my eyes begin to shed tears for you.*

Here he says: "How is it that you have come to dwell — you who were so very timid — in a land where the brave man dwells and is seized with fear?" She was very timid: she was afraid to stay alone in the room, afraid of the dark, afraid of everything; and yet she has come to live in this desolate pit. So this is the second part of the admonition that comes to the visitor of the graves.

This part is what happened in the days of Mu'awiyah, may God be pleased with him. A man came to Syria and saw a funeral bier being carried, and went out with the family; and when they had buried the body, he stood weeping and recited the poet's words:

*O heart, you are deluded about Asma; so remember — and will remembering profit you today? For while a man is among the living, envied his good fortune, all at once he is the grave, swept over by the whirlwinds. The stranger weeps for him who does not know him, while his own kinsman among the living is glad.*

A man among those who had been carrying the bier said to him: do you know who spoke these lines? He said: no, by God. He said: the one who spoke them is the occupant of this grave, and you are the stranger who weeps for him; and he is the one who was envied among the living, and all at once he is the grave, swept over by the whirlwinds. This was among the most remarkable of admonitions.

The third admonition: that a person call to mind the condition of this deceased man's family after his departure from them. They used to be looked upon as living under his protection, and as though he were the one who managed their affairs and attended to their interests; yet he has departed from them and nothing has changed in their lives. They used to think that he was the one who managed and who spent upon them, and that no provision came to them except from him; then he departed, and nothing whatever changed in their affairs. As the poet said:

*The world turned on as though nothing had happened, and no order was thrown out by the turning of time.*

Nothing at all that was, was thrown out. This indicates that God alone is the Manager, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, the Creator, the Provider.

After this comes an admonition at the close: that the visitor to the graves call to mind that the best of his conditions is that he be buried as they were buried — that he die among the Muslims and be prayed over, and return as they returned, and that news of him be cut off; no news reaches from him, no telephone call, no message, no news of any kind, to the people of this world. This is the final, last admonition.

This does not entail wandering among the tombs, walking over them, standing upon them and sitting upon them; these are things the law guards against. The visiting of graves that the law prescribes is that a person stand before the graves so that he sees them and takes admonition from their condition. He ought not to go in among them, nor walk over the graves and sit upon some of them; for it has come in the report of Ali ibn Abi Talib — may God be pleased with him — that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: «That one of you should sit upon live coals, so that they burn his garment and reach his body, is better for him than that he should sit upon a grave.» Likewise walking over the graves and going out across the top of them — all of this is among what ought not to be done. So a person should stand there with the aim of taking admonition and the aim of supplicating.

For the occupants of the graves, if they were believers, benefit from the supplication of one who supplicates for them; and the visitor is the one who gains the greater benefit, through these admonitions we have mentioned. There is no connection whatever between him and the dead beyond this: he cannot derive any benefit from them, nor convey any news to them, nor know anything of their affairs. He benefits only from these admonitions.

As regards travelling to the dead with the aim of visiting, even from afar: travelling to the dead with the aim of visiting is a matter of disagreement among the people of knowledge. What appears to me is that if it is to one's parents, for instance, or the person needs it because of a hardness he finds in his heart — needing to call to mind that he will in all likelihood be buried in this soil, though in truth he does not know where he will be buried: {And no soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die} (Sūrat Luqmān 31:34) — if that is so, then I see no objection to his setting out on a journey for this purpose. But he ought to intend by it a travelling in the path of God, and reflection upon the wonders of God's creation, and admonition; and he should not seek from this visit anything of the kind of thing that people travel for.

For many people travel to the occupants of graves — poor wretches, of whom it is not known whether they are in Paradise or in the Fire — and ask of them what they were unable to do in their own lifetimes, so how much less after their death? God Most High says: {That is God, your Lord; to Him belongs the dominion. And those you call upon besides Him do not possess so much as the skin of a date-stone. If you call upon them they do not hear your call, and if they heard they would not answer you; and on the Day of Resurrection they will disown your associating them with God. And none can inform you like One who is All-Aware.} (Sūrat Fāṭir 35:13–14)

And there has come in the Book of God Most High the words of God addressing Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him), who is God's chosen one among His creation: {Truly you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away in flight} (Sūrat al-Naml 27:80); and there has come in it the words of God Most High: {And the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned} (Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ 21:45); and there has come in it the words of God Most High: {And you are not one who can make those in the graves hear; you are only a warner} (Sūrat Fāṭir 35:22–23). All of this entails that there is no contact at all between the living and the dead. Likewise the words of God Most High: {And behind them is a barrier until the day they are raised up} — "behind them is a barrier", that is, before them is a barrier standing between them and the life of this world and what is in it, until the day they are raised up: {And behind them is a barrier until the day they are raised up. Then when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no ties of kinship between them on that day, nor will they ask after one another. Then those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful; and those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their own souls, abiding in Hell.} (Sūrat al-Muʾminūn 23:100–103)

As for adducing as evidence that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) addressed the people of the well on the day of Badr, this is no proof in the matter; because he knew only by way of revelation that they were hearing, and that this was part of their punishment. It was a punishment for them, not a gladness brought upon them; it is among what increases their punishment. That is why he said: «You are not better able to hear what I say than they are.» This is of the same kind as their punishment, and it is not adduced as evidence with regard to bliss.

In any case, even supposing that the dead do hear, they derive no benefit whatever from hearing anything that reaches them. That they derive no benefit from hearing is a matter of consensus; but whether they hear or not — that is the point of disagreement. As for whether they benefit from hearing, no one has said that they do. They derive no benefit from anything they hear.

## The ruling on one who owes a debt going out to fight

**One who owes a debt and is not able to pay it at present — is he obliged to go out and fight?**

A debt is among the rights of human beings, and these take precedence over the rights of God, because human beings stand in need of their rights, whereas the rights of God — God has no need of them. Therefore he must seek the permission of the creditors for journeys such as hajj, fighting and the like. If they give permission, then there is no objection and the person travels; and if they do not give permission, then he must render to them their rights.

## The ruling on the beard and the moustache

**What is the ruling on shaving the beard and letting the moustache grow?**

It is established from the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) in Sahih al-Bukhari that he said to the two envoys of Chosroes: "But as for me, my Lord has commanded me to let my beard grow and to trim my moustache close." It is established from him in Sahih Muslim that he said: "Let the beards grow full." It is established from him likewise that he said: "Trim the moustaches and let the beards grow full." It is established from him (peace and blessings be upon him) that he said: "Let the beards hang loose." And it is established from him that he said: "Leave the beards be."

All of this means letting the beard grow full and taking from the moustache. Letting the beard grow full means leaving it full. And "beard" means what grows upon the bone of the laḥy, and the laḥy is the lower jaw; so what grows upon it, by the explicit wording of these eight sound reports from the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him), is obliged to be left alone — that is, to be left full. The moustache is what grows upon the upper lip, so taking from it is obligatory, and it is not lawful to leave it to go into the mouth and disfigure the appearance.

But there is disagreement over how much of it must be taken. The majority of the people of knowledge held that what must be taken is what covers the ṭurrah, and that beyond that a person has latitude. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) commanded cutting it right down, so some of the people of knowledge said it ought to be shaved, and Abu Hanifah took this position. Ahmad said it is cut down hard and not shaved. And Malik — may God have mercy on him — said that whoever shaves it is to be disciplined, because he has mutilated himself; this is a mutilation, like shaving off the eyebrow. But he ought to take it down hard, as the Companions of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) used to do.

It is established that al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah — may God be pleased with him — came in upon the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) with his moustache covering his ṭurrah, that is, the edge of the red part on his lip; so he laid him down, brought out a tooth-stick and set it upon his ṭurrah, and took a blade and cut away with it what had grown out of the hair. And al-Mughirah's moustache-trim remained thus ever after, until he met God: whenever al-Mughirah wished to trim his moustache he would bring out his tooth-stick and set it on his mouth, and lie down, and trim — so as to do what the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) had done to him.

## The ruling on eating from the property of one who earns his living by al-raqīq

**If you would go into detail on the matter of eating from the property of one who earns his living by al-raqīq: some of the sisters have husbands who earn by this, so how are they to stop eating from his property?**

We have already mentioned that one who has several sources of earning may be dealt with without qualification, and that his gifts may be accepted; for one the greater part of whose property is lawful — where lawful and forbidden are mixed together in his property — his property may be used. But as for one whose property is entirely from what is forbidden, it is not permissible to accept his gifts except in exchange for a consideration. And if the woman is his wife and finds what makes her independent of his maintenance, then let her make do with that; and if she does not find what makes her independent, then let her take it, and let that be on the ground of necessity (ḍarūrah) only.

## The ruling on covering the feet for women

**If you would speak about socks: one of the sisters, after the instruction to cover the feet, argued against me that you had not declared uncovering the feet forbidden.**

The two feet are a matter of disagreement — whether they are part of what must be covered (ʿawrah) or not — with many positions among the people of knowledge.

The first position: that the feet are part of the ʿawrah, because they are like the rest of the body. Some of the Malikis and some of the Shafi'is held this.

The second position: that the feet are not part of the ʿawrah at all, neither their upper nor their lower surface. This is the position of al-Muzani, of the companions of al-Shafi'i.

The third position: that their lower surface is not part of the ʿawrah and their upper surface is. This is the school of Abu Hanifah.

The fourth position: that if they bear a dye they are part of the ʿawrah, and if they bear no dye they are not.

But the report of Umm Salamah — may God be pleased with her — with which she disputed with the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) when he commanded the men not to go beyond the ankles and said, "what is below the ankles is in the Fire"; she said: "O Messenger of God, what are the women to do with their heels?" He said: "Let them let it down a span." She said: "Then they will be uncovered." He said: "Let them let it down a cubit" — in this there is an absence of strictness on the part of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) in the covering of the feet.

But there is no doubt that covering the feet is a meritorious act (faḍīlah) in any case: whether we say that they are part of the ʿawrah, in which case it is obligatory (wājib); or that they fall below that, in which case it is a matter of prudence and of the noble traits of character. So it is among the meritorious traits of character and deeds, and it ought not to be neglected.
